details: Life Span Study (LSS): Radiation Effects Research Foundation (RERF; joint US-Japan); 86,611 atomic bomb survivors (Hiroshima + Nagasaki) + 27,000 controls; follow-up: 1950-2019 (70+ years); dosimetry: DS02 (Dosimetry System 2002); individual dose estimates using: weapon detonation physics + location at time of bomb + shielding (house/building); dose range: 0 to >5 Gy (mean ~0.15 Gy weighted); primary endpoint: cancer incidence + cancer mortality + non-cancer mortality; main finding: linear dose-response for solid cancers (ERR/Gy = 0.47 at age 70; dose exposure at age 30); leukemia: linear-quadratic model (ERR = α×D + β×D²; peak 3-7yr post-exposure; t½ for excess risk ~10yr); thyroid cancer: ERR/Gy = 0.53 (Thompson 1994; updated Ron 1995); lung: ERR/Gy = 0.32; breast: ERR/Gy = 1.2 females
chernobyl_application: LSS as Chernobyl benchmark: (1) LSS dose range (0-4 Gy) overlaps liquidator range (0-0.5 Gy for most; up to 1+ Gy for roof workers); (2) LSS: acute high-dose-rate exposure; Chernobyl liquidators: protracted exposure over weeks-months; requires DDREF correction (1.5-2.0 for low dose rate); (3) LSS ethnic/social context different from Ukrainian/Belarusian populations; (4) LSS: external gamma + neutron (at Chernobyl: internal component from ingestion/inhalation; reconstructed retrospectively); (5) LSS = basis for LNT model extrapolation to low doses; ERR/Gy derivation from LSS; (6) Chernobyl liquidator leukemia ERR/Gy (1.26; Ivanov 2004) vs LSS leukemia ERR: consistent with LSS + DDREF correction; validates LNT at intermediate doses
source: Pierce 1996 Radiat Res 146:1-27; Preston 2007 Radiat Res 168:1-64; nci_ukraine_thyroid_cohort_REAL.csv; contested_radiation_science_REAL.csv; stochastic_deterministic_effects_REAL.csv

details: Excess Relative Risk (ERR) vs Excess Absolute Risk (EAR): ERR = (observed - expected) / expected / dose = proportional to background cancer rate; ERR model: cancer risk = background × (1 + ERR × dose); EAR = (observed - expected) / person-years / dose = absolute excess cases per person-year-Gy; EAR model: cancer risk = background + EAR × dose; DIFFERENCE: ERR predicts higher absolute risk in high-baseline-risk populations (older; smokers; high-incidence countries); EAR predicts constant absolute excess regardless of background; example: thyroid cancer ERR/Gy = 7.7 (post-Chernobyl children; Tronko 2006) = highly elevated relative; EAR = 2.1 cases/10⁴ person-year-Gy (absolute); difference matters for risk projection: WHO/IARC uses ERR model for thyroid cancer; gives higher absolute numbers in countries with high pre-existing thyroid cancer rates (US > Japan > Belarus for pre-existing rates)
chernobyl_application: Chernobyl application: UNSCEAR uses ERR model primarily; projected thyroid cancer deaths = ERR/Gy × background thyroid cancer mortality × dose × population; IARC 2006 Chernobyl report: projects 16,000 excess fatal cancers (all types) using ERR model + DDREF=2; UNSCEAR: 4,000-6,600; DIFFERENCE = model choice (ERR vs EAR) + DDREF value + dose reconstruction method; for solid tumors other than thyroid: ERR lower confidence (underpowered in liquidator cohorts); leukemia: ERR well-established (ERR/Gy=1.52 for liquidators; Ivanov 2004); thyroid: ERR/Gy=7.7 (children); well-established
source: Brenner 2011 Proc Natl Acad Sci; UNSCEAR 2008 Annex D; IARC 2006; liquidator_health_outcomes_REAL.csv; nci_ukraine_thyroid_cohort_REAL.csv

details: Linear No-Threshold (LNT) model derivation: mechanistic basis: DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs): ~40 DSBs/Gy; at 1 mGy = 0.04 DSBs/cell (stochastic; some cells receive 0; some receive 1); at low dose: probability of misrepair SAME as at high dose (linear with dose); evidence: (1) LSS data: best-fit for solid cancers: linear at 100-4000 mGy (Pierce 1996); linear model not rejected below 100 mGy (insufficient power); (2) LSS excess cancers statistically significant down to ~200 mGy; (3) Techa River cohort (USSR chronic low dose; Kossenko 1997): excess leukemia at ~60 mGy cumulative; (4) UK radiation workers study: excess leukemia at <100 mGy; (5) Mechanistic: DSB rate α dose from first principles; threshold would require explaining WHY misrepair probability changes → no such mechanism found; DDREF = 1.5-2.0: accounts for dose-rate effect (lower repair capacity utilization at low dose rate → more complete repair)
chernobyl_application: LNT in Chernobyl context: primary source of controversy; ICRP adopts LNT + DDREF for radiological protection; UNSCEAR: uses LNT cautiously; WHO: LNT basis; critics (e.g. Raabe 2010; Scott 2008; SARI group): LNT predicts 6,600-25,000 excess cancer deaths from Chernobyl; LNT proponents: these projections are consistent with dose data; LNT critics claim threshold exists → far fewer deaths; Chernobyl data resolution: thyroid cancer in children (confirmed 6000+ cases; few disputed) DOES demonstrate dose-response; for solid tumors other than thyroid at low dose (<100 mSv): insufficient statistical power to confirm or reject LNT empirically in Chernobyl data; contested_radiation_science_REAL.csv has full LNT controversy

details: Cohort study design in Chernobyl epidemiology: Prospective cohort: group defined by exposure → followed over time → outcomes recorded; RNMDR (Russian National Medical Dosimetric Registry): 200,000 liquidators; established 1991; annual examination protocol; annual: blood count; CBC; clinical examination; every 3yr: full biochemistry; ECG; every 5yr: neurological assessment; endpoint: cancer incidence + mortality + non-cancer morbidity; strengths: prospective; large; complete follow-up; individual dose records (even if imperfect); weaknesses: Soviet dosimetry falsification (requires correction); healthy worker effect (only workers; excludes severely ill from initial response); loss-to-follow-up ~25% (dissolution of USSR made tracking difficult); Kashcheev 2015 CVD analysis (n=53,772): shows dose-response for CVD (ERR/Gy=0.47); validates radiation CVD hypothesis; NCI UkrAm (Ukraine + America joint): 13,127 childhood thyroid cancer subjects; ERR/Gy=1.91 (Tronko 2006)
chernobyl_application: Case-control study: selected cancer cases + matched controls; assess prior exposure; nested case-control: cases within cohort; efficient for rare outcomes; Chernobyl thyroid cancer case-control: Ron 1995 (n=350 cases + 1000 controls); exposure assessment: 400,000 Soviet thyroid measurements 1986 (mostly too late; unreliable); RADRUE reconstruction for subset; ERR/Gy by age: children 0-4yr: ERR/Gy = 10-15; children 10-15yr: ERR/Gy = 3-5; adults: ERR/Gy = 0.4-0.7 (consistent with LSS); Belarusian thyroid cancer: 6,800+ cases in people exposed before age 18; SIR (standardized incidence ratio) evacuees = 13.0 (13× expected); confirms dose-response beyond statistical doubt; see thyroid_cancer_timeseries_REAL.csv
source: Ivanov 2004 Radiat Environ Biophys; Tronko 2006 BMJ; Kashcheev 2015 Radiat Environ Biophys; UNSCEAR 2008; nci_ukraine_thyroid_cohort_REAL.csv; liquidator_health_outcomes_REAL.csv

details: Confounding factors in Chernobyl epidemiology: (1) Healthy worker effect: liquidators were actively employed at time of assignment → healthier than general population at baseline → underestimation of radiation effects (healthy worker 'survivor bias'); (2) Alcohol use: 60% of liquidators reported heavy alcohol use (survey data; Ivanov 1997); alcohol = CVD risk factor; confounds CVD analysis; addressed by: multivariate adjustment; dose-response analysis (radiation effect independent of alcohol if dose-response confirmed); (3) Smoking: 56% current smokers in RNMDR cohort (vs ~40% Ukrainian general population); lung cancer confounding; (4) Socioeconomic factors: many liquidators from lower SES; worse baseline health; healthcare access; (5) Psychological stress: radiation-related anxiety → elevated cortisol → CVD pathway; (6) Dosimetry uncertainty: measurement error → dose misclassification → usually attenuates ERR toward zero (Berkson error type)
chernobyl_application: Addressing confounding: (1) Dose-response analysis: if confounder does NOT have dose-response relationship, radiation signal appears as dose trend above confounding baseline; (2) Matched case-control: match on smoking/alcohol/age/sex; (3) EPR dosimetry: replaces falsified badge records with objective measurement; reduces dose misclassification; (4) RADRUE Monte Carlo: propagates dose uncertainty properly (attenuated ERR corrected by regression calibration); (5) International comparison: Ukrainian + Russian + Belarusian liquidator cohorts show consistent ERR/Gy within uncertainty bands → consistent findings across different countries + registries = reduces confounding concern; bottom line: dose-response for leukemia (ERR/Gy=1.26-1.52) and thyroid cancer (ERR/Gy=1.91) confirmed beyond reasonable doubt; CVD ERR/Gy=0.47 with dose-response = likely real

details: Statistical power analysis for Chernobyl liquidator cancer studies: cohort size: ~600,000 total liquidators globally; ~200,000 in RNMDR; mean dose: ~117 mSv; 40-year follow-up; cancer mortality rate in Soviet/post-Soviet males ~50yr old: ~350/100,000/yr; expected excess cancer deaths at ERR/Gy=0.5: 600,000 × 0.117 Gy × 0.5 × 350/100,000 = ~123 excess cancer deaths/year (above ~2,100 expected); statistical detection: requires ~(Z_α + Z_β)²/(O/E) years of follow-up for 80% power; for solid tumors: ~20yr follow-up for ERR/Gy=0.5 detection; leukemia: shorter latency + higher ERR → detected sooner; LEUKEMIA: powered to detect ERR/Gy > 0.3 at 2σ (alpha=0.05; beta=0.20) with n=200,000 and 20yr follow-up; solid tumors except thyroid: underpowered for ERR/Gy <0.5 in single cohort; thyroid cancer: sufficient power (SIR=13×; ERR clearly significant even in small cohorts due to large relative risk)
chernobyl_application: Why some radiation effects in liquidators are NOT detectable: solid tumors (lung; colon; breast) with ERR/Gy=0.3-0.5: would require 2-4 million person-years of follow-up at liquidator dose levels; RNMDR + NCI UkrAm combined: ~10 million person-years; theoretical detection possible BUT: confounding (smoking; alcohol) adds noise that masks signal; dose uncertainty (factor 2-3 GSD) attenuates estimated ERR by ~40%; therefore: absence of significant solid tumor excess in liquidators ≠ radiation is safe at these doses; it means: underpowered study + measurement error + confounding; this is the central challenge of low-dose radiation epidemiology; solution: pooled analyses (International Radiation Workers Study; INWORKS: 300,000 workers; Leuraud 2015)
source: Pierce 1996; UNSCEAR 2008; Leuraud 2015 Lancet Haematol; birth_defects_general_health_REAL.csv; contested_radiation_science_REAL.csv

details: DDREF (Dose and Dose-Rate Effectiveness Factor): ratio of cancer risk per unit dose at low dose AND low dose rate vs high dose/high dose rate (as measured in LSS); DDREF = ERR/Gy(high dose/rate) / ERR/Gy(low dose/rate); ICRP recommendation: DDREF = 2 for gamma radiation (ICRP 103 2007); UNSCEAR: DDREF = 1.5-2 (range of uncertainty); mechanistic basis: at low dose rate, cells have time to repair sublethal damage before next hit; NHEJ + HR repair deplete misrepair probability → fewer fixed DSBs per unit dose; experimental evidence: in vitro mammalian cells: DDREF = 2-10 (higher DDREF in very sensitive assays); animal carcinogenesis: DDREF = 2-5; LSS itself (single acute exposure): requires DDREF correction to apply to chronic exposure of liquidators; Techa River chronic exposure cohort: independent DDREF estimate ~2 (consistent with ICRP value)
chernobyl_application: Chernobyl DDREF application: liquidators received protracted exposure over weeks-months (not instantaneous like A-bomb); therefore: ERR projected from LSS data should be divided by DDREF before comparing with liquidator data; LSS solid tumor ERR/Gy = 0.47; liquidator solid tumor ERR/Gy ≈ 0.1-0.2 (not statistically significant); ratio = 2.4-4.7 = consistent with DDREF = 2-5; supports LNT + DDREF framework; controversy: some scientists argue DDREF should be applied to BOTH low-dose and protracted exposure (liquidators); others argue liquidator doses too brief to qualify as 'low dose rate'; current UNSCEAR position: DDREF applicable to liquidator doses below ~100 mGy

details: Attributable fraction (AF): proportion of cancer cases in exposed population attributable to radiation: AF = (ERR × dose) / (1 + ERR × dose); for individual case with dose D and cancer type with ERR/Gy: AF = probability that this individual's cancer was radiation-induced; example: liquidator with thyroid cancer; dose = 300 mGy; ERR/Gy = 1.91 (Tronko 2006): AF = 1.91×0.3 / (1 + 1.91×0.3) = 0.573/1.573 = 0.36 = 36% probability radiation-induced; example: child evacuee with thyroid cancer; dose = 2 Gy; ERR/Gy = 7.7: AF = 7.7×2 / (1 + 7.7×2) = 15.4/16.4 = 0.94 = 94% probability radiation-induced; used in: legal compensation decisions; policy analysis; individual patient counseling; population burden attribution (total excess cases = AF × total cases); AF NOT = certainty of causation (stochastic; probabilistic)
chernobyl_application: Attributable fraction in Chernobyl compensation: Ukraine Law No. 796-XII (1991): compensation based on 'probability of radiation causation'; AF≥0.5 = compensation; AF<0.5 = no compensation (by some interpretations); WHO 2006: overall 0.5 AF threshold = ~3,500 diagnosed thyroid cancers by 2005 = radiation-attributable; total cancers: ~6,000 by 2005 → ~3,500 attributable (AF ~0.58 average); HOWEVER: individual AF varies enormously by dose: 5 Gy thyroid dose: AF=97%; 50 mGy: AF=28%; 5 mGy: AF=4%; fairness issues: low-dose individuals receive no compensation despite statistical causation contribution; compensation systems generally use threshold approaches (AF>0.5) = simpler but imprecise
source: Ron 1995 Radiat Res; Tronko 2006 BMJ; UNSCEAR 2008; stochastic_deterministic_effects_REAL.csv; nci_ukraine_thyroid_cohort_REAL.csv
